parts.q: Which organelle normally modifies proteins received from rough ER?
ms: B: Golgi apparatus.

parts.q: Which cell component is found in a typical bacterium?
ms: C: 70S ribosomes.

parts.q: A cell image is 12 mm wide and the cell is 30 µm wide. What is magnification?
Which reaction forms a peptide bond?
ms: A: Condensation between amino acids.

parts.q: Which feature distinguishes cellulose from amylose?
ms: A: It contains β-glucose.

parts.q: Which change directly raises facilitated diffusion rate before carrier saturation?
ms: A: A steeper substrate gradient.

parts.q: Which enzyme adds complementary DNA nucleotides during replication?
ms: B: DNA polymerase.

parts.q: What separates in mitotic anaphase?
ms: B: Sister chromatids.

parts.q: Which factor shifts an adult haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
ms: A: Higher carbon dioxide concentration.

parts.q: Which event initiates the normal cardiac electrical cycle?
ms: B: SAN excitation.

parts.q: Which process does a shoot potometer directly estimate?
ms: A: Water uptake.

parts.q: Where is most urea produced?
ms: C: Liver.

parts.q: Which event depolarises an axon during the action-potential upstroke?
ms: A: Sodium entry.

parts.q: What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?
ms: B: Oxygen.

parts.q: Which process produces ATP without reduced NADP or oxygen in a chloroplast?
ms: A: Cyclic photophosphorylation.

questions.title: A secretory cell and an enzyme investigation
questions.stem: A student studies enzyme-secreting cells. A cell measures 28 graticule divisions; calibration shows 10 divisions represent 15 µm. An enzyme from the cells is tested at substrate concentrations of 1, 2, 4 and 8 mmol dm⁻³. Mean initial rates are 2.0, 3.5, 5.0 and 5.2 arbitrary units min⁻¹ respectively, using the same enzyme concentration.

parts.q: Calculate the cell length in µm and explain why the calibration must be repeated after changing the objective.
ms: One division represents 15/10 = 1.5 µm.
The cell is 28 × 1.5 = 42 µm long.
Changing objective magnification changes the specimen length represented by each division.

parts.q: Explain three structural adaptations expected in a protein-secreting cell.
ms: Extensive rough ER with ribosomes synthesises proteins.
A developed Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins.
Many mitochondria provide ATP for synthesis and vesicle movement.

parts.q: Explain the initial-rate pattern as substrate concentration increases.
ms: At low concentration, more substrate increases successful enzyme–substrate encounters.
At high concentration most active sites are occupied.
With fixed enzyme concentration, substrate is no longer the main limiting factor and rate approaches a maximum.

parts.q: Describe three improvements to the validity or reliability of the enzyme comparison.
ms: Use a buffer to keep pH constant.
Use a controlled water bath to maintain temperature.
Use independent repeats and compare initial gradients with a measure of spread.

questions.title: Replication and dividing root cells
questions.stem: A root-tip sample contains 240 cells, including 36 in mitosis. The organism has a diploid chromosome number of 12. A template DNA segment is TAC GGA TTT.

parts.q: Calculate the mitotic index and state one assumption needed to use it to estimate the fraction of cell-cycle time spent in mitosis. Give the mitotic index as a decimal.
ms: Mitotic index = 36/240.
The index is 0.15 or 15%.
The sampled population is representative and approximately steady-state with comparable cell-cycle behaviour.

parts.q: Write the complementary mRNA sequence and explain why replication is described as semi-conservative.
ms: The mRNA sequence is AUG CCU AAA.
Each original DNA strand acts as a template for a new strand.
Each resulting DNA double helix contains one old and one new strand.

parts.q: Compare mitosis with meiosis for this organism.
ms: Mitosis maintains 12 chromosomes in each daughter nucleus.
Normal meiosis produces haploid nuclei with six chromosomes.
Mitosis involves one nuclear division whereas meiosis involves two after one replication.
Meiosis includes homologous pairing and crossing over that contribute to variation.

questions.title: Exercise, circulation and gas exchange
questions.stem: An athlete has heart rate 72 min⁻¹ and stroke volume 75 cm³ at rest. During exercise these become 150 min⁻¹ and 110 cm³. At an oxygen partial pressure of 5 kPa, haemoglobin saturation is 75% in one condition and 60% in a condition with higher carbon dioxide.

parts.q: Calculate cardiac output during exercise in dm³ min⁻¹ and its increase from rest.
ms: Exercise output = 150 × 110 = 16 500 cm³ min⁻¹ = 16.5 dm³ min⁻¹.
Rest output = 72 × 75 = 5400 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.4 dm³ min⁻¹.
The increase is 11.1 dm³ min⁻¹.

parts.q: Use the saturation data to explain the effect of higher carbon dioxide on oxygen delivery.
ms: At the same partial pressure saturation falls by 15 percentage points.
Higher carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin affinity, shifting the curve right.
This promotes unloading of oxygen in actively respiring tissues.

parts.q: Explain how three alveolar features maintain rapid oxygen uptake.
ms: Large total surface area permits more simultaneous diffusion.
Thin alveolar and capillary barriers reduce diffusion distance.
Ventilation and perfusion maintain the concentration gradient.

parts.q: Explain coordinated ventricular excitation and contraction.
ms: Excitation is initiated at the sinoatrial node and spreads through atria.
The atrioventricular node delays transmission until after atrial contraction.
The bundle of His conducts excitation towards the apex.
Purkyne tissue spreads excitation so ventricles contract from the apex upwards.

questions.title: Water and assimilate transport in a plant
questions.stem: A potometer capillary has cross-sectional area 0.40 mm². A bubble moves 60 mm in 5 minutes. The experiment is repeated with a fan directed at the shoot. The same plant exports sucrose from mature leaves to growing roots.

parts.q: Calculate water uptake rate in mm³ min⁻¹ and give one reason why it need not exactly equal transpiration rate.
ms: Volume = 0.40 × 60 = 24 mm³.
Rate = 24/5 = 4.8 mm³ min⁻¹.
Some absorbed water is retained for growth or used in metabolism, so uptake is a proxy.

parts.q: Explain why the fan may increase the measured rate if other variables and stomatal opening remain similar.
ms: Moving air removes the humid boundary layer.
This steepens the water-vapour gradient between leaf and air.
Faster diffusion increases evaporation and water loss.

parts.q: Explain how mature leaves supply sucrose to roots through phloem, using an apoplastic loading model.
ms: Companion-cell proton pumps use ATP to establish a proton gradient.
Proton–sucrose cotransport helps load sucrose at the source.
Sucrose accumulation lowers sieve-tube water potential.
Water enters by osmosis and raises hydrostatic pressure.
A pressure gradient drives bulk flow towards the sink.
Unloading and use of sucrose at roots help maintain the gradient.

questions.title: Kidney regulation during dehydration
questions.stem: After prolonged exercise without drinking, an individual has a lower blood water potential and a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. The individual has normal kidney function.

parts.q: Explain why glomerular filtrate contains glucose but very little large plasma protein.
ms: High hydrostatic pressure drives water and small solutes across the filtration barrier.
Glucose is small enough to cross.
The barrier restricts most large proteins and blood cells.

parts.q: Explain four steps linking reduced blood water potential to concentrated urine.
ms: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect the lower water potential.
ADH release from the posterior pituitary increases.
Aquaporin insertion increases collecting-duct water permeability.
More water returns to blood by osmosis down the medullary gradient, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

parts.q: Explain how liver metabolism and kidney function together remove excess amino nitrogen.
ms: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver.
The amino groups generate ammonia.
The liver converts toxic ammonia to less toxic urea.
Urea travels in blood to kidneys and is excreted in urine after filtration and processing.

questions.title: Energy metabolism in cells
questions.stem: A mitochondrial preparation consumes 15.0 µmol O₂ while producing 10.5 µmol CO₂. A separate photosynthesis experiment shows a plateau in carbon uptake at high light intensity. Both experiments include appropriate controls.

parts.q: Calculate respiratory quotient and interpret the result cautiously.
ms: RQ = CO₂ produced / O₂ consumed.
This is consistent with substantial lipid oxidation under the stated conditions, rather than uniquely proving a pure substrate.

parts.q: Explain why cyanide inhibition of the terminal electron-transfer step reduces mitochondrial ATP synthesis.
ms: Electron transfer to oxygen is inhibited.
Proton pumping and the maintained proton gradient decline.
ATP synthase consequently has less proton-motive driving force.

parts.q: Suggest how to test whether carbon dioxide supply limits photosynthesis at the high-light plateau.
ms: Increase carbon dioxide while keeping high light and temperature constant.
Measure comparable net carbon-uptake rates with repeats.
An increased rate supports carbon dioxide limitation in the original conditions.

parts.q: Explain how light-dependent reactions provide the materials needed for carbohydrate synthesis in the Calvin cycle.
ms: Light excites electrons in photosynthetic reaction centres.
Water photolysis replaces electrons and releases protons and oxygen.
Electron transport supports a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase.
Electrons and protons reduce NADP.
ATP and reduced NADP support reduction of GP to TP.
ATP also supports RuBP regeneration, while some TP contributes to carbohydrate synthesis.

questions.title: Nervous signalling and muscle contraction
questions.stem: A nerve stimulates a skeletal-muscle fibre through a cholinergic neuromuscular junction. A drug blocks presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels without directly affecting axonal sodium channels.

parts.q: Explain generation and restoration of an axonal action potential.
ms: Threshold opens voltage-gated sodium channels.
Sodium entry depolarises the membrane.
Sodium-channel inactivation and potassium-channel opening cause repolarisation.
A refractory period limits immediate re-excitation.

parts.q: Predict the drug effect at the neuromuscular junction and explain its mechanism.
ms: Axonal impulses can still reach the terminal because sodium channels remain functional.
Less calcium enters the presynaptic terminal.
Vesicle fusion and acetylcholine release are reduced.
Postsynaptic excitation and muscle activation are reduced.

parts.q: Explain how calcium and ATP permit the sliding-filament cycle.
ms: Calcium binds troponin.
Tropomyosin moves to expose actin binding sites.
Myosin crossbridges bind and undergo power strokes.
ATP binding detaches myosin and hydrolysis re-energises the head for another cycle.

parts.q: Which molecules form most of a plasma-membrane bilayer?
ms: B: Phospholipids.

parts.q: Which test gives a lilac or purple result with protein?
ms: B: Biuret.

parts.q: Which sequence is complementary mRNA to template DNA CCA? The template triplet is written 3′→5′ and the RNA triplet must be 5′→3′.
ms: A: GGU.

parts.q: Which creates new alleles?
ms: C: Mutation.

parts.q: Which cell type secretes antibody?
ms: A: Plasma cell.

parts.q: Which describes passive immunity?
ms: A: Antibodies are transferred to a recipient.
opts: Antibodies are transferred to a recipient
The recipient always forms lasting memory
Only cytotoxic T cells are transferred

parts.q: Which is a protoctist pathogen?
ms: A: Plasmodium.

parts.q: Which two ranks form a binomial name?
ms: B: Genus and species.

parts.q: Under Hardy–Weinberg, p = 0.8 and q = 0.2. What is 2pq?
What does DNA ligase do?
ms: A: Joins DNA fragments.

parts.q: DNA migrates towards which electrode during electrophoresis?
ms: B: Positive.

parts.q: Which is an ex-situ conservation method?
ms: A: Seed banking.

parts.q: Which process converts ammonium to nitrite and nitrate?
ms: B: Nitrification.

parts.q: Which is the correct productivity relationship?
ms: A: NPP = GPP − producer respiration.

parts.q: Which test is appropriate for independent offspring category counts against fixed expected proportions?
ms: A: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit.

questions.title: A new respiratory pathogen
questions.stem: A bacterium spreads through respiratory droplets. A vaccine contains a purified bacterial surface antigen. In a laboratory comparison, susceptible bacteria decline strongly after antibiotic exposure, while a small resistant population survives and increases in frequency.

parts.q: Explain the response that produces specific circulating antibodies after vaccination.
ms: An appropriate B-cell receptor recognises the vaccine antigen.
Activation, usually with helper-T-cell support, leads to clonal expansion.
Some B-cell descendants become plasma cells.
Plasma cells secrete antibodies with binding sites complementary to the antigen.

parts.q: Compare active vaccination with passive antibody transfer.
ms: Vaccination stimulates the recipient’s own adaptive immune response.
It can establish memory populations and a faster secondary response.
Passive transfer supplies ready-made antibodies for immediate protection.
Passive antibodies are eventually lost and do not themselves establish the same antigen-specific memory response.

parts.q: Explain the increase in antibiotic resistance without describing a directed response to need.
ms: Mutation or acquired genes provide heritable resistance in some cells.
Antibiotic exposure inhibits susceptible cells more strongly.
Resistant cells survive and reproduce, passing on resistance.
Their relative frequency rises through selection.

questions.title: Comparing grassland biodiversity
questions.stem:
Equal sampling effort records 40 individuals at each of two sites.

SpeciesSite ASite B
11028
2104
3104
4104

Use D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².

parts.q: Calculate D for Site A.
ms: Each species has n/N = 10/40 = 0.25.

parts.q: Calculate D for Site B and compare the communities.
ms: Species richness is equal at four species.
Site A has greater evenness and the higher diversity index under this definition.

parts.q: Design a field investigation of how plant distribution changes with distance from a path.
ms: Use systematic quadrats along transects extending away from the path.
Use a consistent quadrat size and recording method.
Repeat transects at independently selected locations.
Measure distance and relevant abiotic factors such as light or soil moisture.
Control sampling season and effort, and identify species consistently.
Analyse trends with variation and avoid concluding causation from correlation alone.

questions.title: A two-locus inheritance model
questions.stem: A plant’s pigment pathway produces colour only when at least one functional allele is present at both unlinked loci A and B. An AaBb × AaBb cross produces 190 coloured and 130 colourless offspring. The model predicts a 9:7 phenotypic ratio. Use χ² = Σ[(O − E)²/E]. The 5% critical value at one degree of freedom is 3.84.

parts.q: Explain why the expected phenotypic ratio is 9:7 rather than 9:3:3:1.
ms: Both A and B function are required for colour.
Nine sixteenths are A_B_ and are coloured.
The remaining aaB_, A_bb and aabb groups together form seven sixteenths and are colourless.

parts.q: Calculate expected counts, calculate χ² and state the conclusion.
ms: Expected counts are 180 coloured and 140 colourless.
1.27 is below the critical value 3.84.
Do not reject the 9:7 model’s null hypothesis; the data are consistent with it but do not prove it.

parts.q: In a separate large population, a recessive phenotype frequency is 0.16. Use Hardy–Weinberg to calculate heterozygote frequency and state two assumptions.
ms: Heterozygote frequency = 2pq = 0.48.
Mating is random and the population is sufficiently large to minimise drift.
Selection, migration and mutation do not materially alter the locus during the modelled interval.

questions.title: Investigating a candidate gene
questions.stem: A laboratory amplifies a 600-base-pair target, separates products by electrophoresis and places a human coding sequence in a bacterial expression vector. Starting with 12 target molecules, assume ideal doubling for the calculation only.

parts.q: Calculate target copies after six ideal PCR cycles and give one reason real yields can differ.
ms: Copies = 12 × 2⁶.
The predicted count is 768.
Real efficiency can be reduced by limited reagents, incomplete amplification or inhibition.

parts.q: Explain how a gel distinguishes 300-base-pair and 600-base-pair DNA fragments.
ms: DNA has a net negative charge from its phosphate backbone.
It moves towards the positive electrode.
Smaller fragments pass through the gel matrix more readily and normally travel farther.
A size marker allows comparison under the same running conditions.

parts.q: Describe how to obtain and express an intron-free human coding sequence in bacteria.
ms: Obtain mature mRNA from cells expressing the target gene.
Use reverse transcriptase to produce cDNA.
Join a suitable coding sequence into an expression vector using an appropriate DNA-assembly method.
Include a bacterial-compatible promoter and replication features.
Introduce the vector into host cells and select or screen successful clones.
Confirm the desired protein is expressed and functional rather than relying only on marker survival.

questions.title: An industrial enzyme process
questions.stem: A company compares free and immobilised lactase. Both treatments contain comparable enzyme activity under a standard assay. Product collected from a continuous immobilised-enzyme column initially rises, then falls after prolonged use.

parts.q: Give two benefits and one limitation of immobilising lactase.
ms: The enzyme can be retained and reused.
It is easier to separate enzyme from product.
Diffusion into the support or altered activity can limit the reaction rate.

parts.q: Suggest three factors to investigate when the column output declines.
ms: Check enzyme stability or loss of functional activity over time.
Check substrate supply, flow rate and diffusion through the support.
Check contamination, pH and temperature against the intended conditions.

parts.q: Explain how an aerobic microbial culture used to produce the enzyme should be controlled.
ms: Maintain aseptic equipment and nutrient supply to reduce contamination.
Regulate temperature to support growth and enzyme function.
Control pH because cellular and enzyme activity depend on it.
Supply oxygen and mix to distribute it throughout the culture.
Monitor growth and harvest at a stage appropriate to the desired product.
Use independent quality checks for product identity, purity and activity.

questions.title: Production and nutrient cycling
questions.stem: A wetland has GPP 4200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and producer respiration 1800 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Herbivore production is 288 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Waterlogged patches have less oxygen than well-aerated soil.

parts.q: Calculate NPP and the efficiency of transfer from producer NPP to herbivore production.
ms: Efficiency = 288/2400 × 100.
The efficiency is 12%.

parts.q: Explain why producer NPP exceeds herbivore production.
ms: Some producer biomass is not eaten.
Some ingested material is not digested or absorbed and is egested.
Some absorbed energy is used in respiration and dissipated.
Other losses, such as excretion, leave less material and energy for herbivore growth.

parts.q: Explain how decomposition and low oxygen conditions can affect nitrogen availability.
ms: Decomposition releases ammonium from organic nitrogen through ammonification.
Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrite and nitrate where conditions support the process.
Low oxygen can favour denitrification that converts nitrate to nitrogen gas.
This can reduce nitrate available for plant uptake.

questions.title: Managing a fragmented species
questions.stem: A mammal survives in three small isolated woodland populations. Managers propose habitat corridors, captive breeding and later reintroduction. A camera survey suggests a population increase after a corridor opens, but food availability also rises during the same period.

parts.q: Explain why small isolated populations can lose genetic diversity.
ms: Drift can remove alleles by chance in small populations.
Restricted gene flow limits replacement of lost alleles.
Inbreeding can increase homozygosity and expose harmful recessive alleles.

parts.q: Explain why the camera survey alone cannot show that the corridor caused the increase.
ms: Food availability is a confounding variable that may influence survival or reproduction.
Detection probability or sampling effort may also change apparent abundance.
A replicated controlled or carefully matched before–after comparison would provide stronger evidence.

parts.q: Evaluate the combined corridor and captive-breeding strategy.
ms: Corridors can support movement, gene flow and recolonisation.
Habitat protection addresses threats in the natural ecological context.
Captive breeding can provide an insurance population or animals for release.
Breeding should manage relatedness and retain genetic diversity.
Corridors and releases may also spread disease or create welfare and ecological problems.
Success needs suitable habitat, threat reduction and long-term monitoring against explicit recovery goals.

title: Set 1 · Unified biology
subject: Biology
coverage: Practical design, t-test calculation, ecology and molecular biology

questions.title: A plant enzyme under salt stress
questions.stem: Researchers measure initial enzyme activity from five independently sampled control plants and five salt-treated plants. Mean activities are 3.0 and 2.0 µmol min⁻¹, with sample SD 0.50 µmol min⁻¹ in both groups. Assume normality and equal population variance are reasonable. Use t = |x̄₁ − x̄₂| / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Use 8 degrees of freedom and a two-tailed 5% critical value of 2.306. One control extract produces 0.9 µmol product in its first 18 seconds.
questions.topic: Enzymes; protein structure; experimental design; statistics

parts.q: Calculate the extract’s mean rate over 18 seconds in µmol min⁻¹.
ms: Convert 18 s to 0.30 min.
Calculate 0.9/0.30.
The rate is 3.0 µmol min⁻¹.

parts.q: Explain why altered enzyme tertiary structure may reduce activity.
ms: Changes in R-group interactions can alter the folded shape.
The active-site shape or chemical environment may change.
Substrate binding or catalysis can become less effective.

parts.q: Calculate t and interpret the test.
ms: 3.16 exceeds 2.306, so reject the null of equal population mean activities at the 5% level.
Evidence supports a difference under the assumptions but does not prove its molecular cause.

parts.q: Describe four design features needed to attribute the difference to salt rather than confounding.
ms: Randomly allocate comparable plants to treatment and control.
Keep growth conditions, age and sampled tissue comparable apart from salt.
Standardise extraction, tissue-mass basis and assay pH and temperature.
Use independent biological replicates rather than only repeat readings of one extract.

questions.title: Flooding, drought and carbon gain
questions.stem: Two woodland areas alternate between waterlogging and dry conditions. In a chamber, illuminated shoots show net oxygen production of 8.0 cm³ h⁻¹; in darkness, equal tissue consumes 2.0 cm³ O₂ h⁻¹. Assume for calculation that respiration in light equals respiration in darkness. During drought, stomatal aperture decreases.

parts.q: Explain the Calvin-cycle steps by which carbon dioxide contributes to organic molecules.
ms: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide to RuBP, producing GP after an unstable intermediate splits.
ATP and reduced NADP support conversion of GP to TP.
Some TP contributes to organic synthesis while most regenerates RuBP using ATP.

parts.q: Estimate gross oxygen production in light and state a limitation.
ms: Gross production = net production + respiratory uptake.
The estimate is 8.0 + 2.0 = 10.0 cm³ h⁻¹.
It depends on respiration being unchanged between light and darkness.

parts.q: Explain how stomatal closure affects water loss and can restrict carbon gain.
ms: Closure increases resistance to water-vapour diffusion and reduces transpiration.
It reduces evaporative demand driving xylem tension.
It also restricts carbon dioxide entry.
Reduced carbon supply can limit carbon fixation and carbohydrate production.

parts.q: Explain how waterlogging may alter nitrogen supply and community composition.
ms: Low oxygen can limit aerobic root and microbial processes.
Suitable low-oxygen conditions can favour denitrification.
Conversion of nitrate to nitrogen gas reduces available nitrate.
Species differ in tolerance and resource use, changing relative survival or growth.

questions.title: Producing an antigen for a vaccine
questions.stem: A laboratory identifies a viral surface-protein coding sequence and expresses an appropriate version in a host-cell system. The purified protein is investigated as a vaccine antigen. A later viral population has an altered surface-protein sequence.

parts.q: Explain how vaccination can produce a faster response after later exposure.
ms: Specific lymphocytes recognise antigen and are activated.
Clonal expansion produces effector cells.
Memory lymphocytes persist.
Re-exposure generates a faster and larger antigen-specific response.

parts.q: Explain three requirements for PCR amplification.
ms: Primers anneal to sequences flanking the target.
A thermostable DNA polymerase extends primers.
Thermal cycling separates strands, permits annealing and supports extension with free nucleotides.

parts.q: Explain four issues in expressing and purifying a functional antigen.
ms: The coding sequence and regulatory features must suit the host.
The protein must fold appropriately and receive necessary modifications.
Successful constructs must be selected or screened and expression verified.
Quality checks must assess identity, contamination and retained antigenic function.

parts.q: Explain how immune selection can increase a variant with altered antibody recognition.
ms: Mutation supplies heritable sequence variation.
Less effectively recognised variants may reproduce or transmit more successfully.
Their frequency can increase without mutations being directed by the need for immune evasion.

questions.title: An inhibitor affects an active animal
questions.stem: A compound inhibits the terminal mitochondrial electron-transfer step without directly blocking ion channels or myosin. Researchers investigate a repeatedly stimulated skeletal muscle and the systems supplying it.

parts.q: Explain why the inhibitor reduces oxidative ATP synthesis.
ms: Oxygen cannot accept electrons normally at the terminal step.
Carriers remain reduced and normal electron flow is restricted.
Electron-transport-linked proton pumping declines.
The proton gradient is not adequately maintained.
ATP synthase has less proton-motive driving force.

parts.q: Explain why prolonged ATP shortage impairs neuronal signalling despite unblocked channels.
ms: The sodium–potassium pump requires ATP.
Reduced pumping allows sodium and potassium gradients to deteriorate.
Resting potential and the driving forces for ionic currents are affected.
Reliable impulse generation and recovery can fail.

parts.q: Explain ATP requirements in muscle and why glycolysis may temporarily continue.
ms: ATP binding enables myosin detachment and further cycling.
ATP supports calcium pumping during relaxation.
Reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD.
Glycolysis can then make a small ATP supply by substrate-level phosphorylation, insufficient for sustained normal high output.

parts.q: Explain why increased cardiac output cannot fully overcome the inhibitor.
ms: Higher output can increase oxygen delivery.
The inhibited terminal pathway cannot use that oxygen normally.
The limitation is cellular utilisation, so supply alone does not restore oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.title: A threatened butterfly population
questions.stem: Investigators mark and release 40 butterflies. After mixing, they capture 50, including 10 marked individuals. A separate large reference population has a recessive phenotype frequency of 0.04. The threatened population becomes fragmented into small isolated groups.

parts.q: Estimate population size and state three assumptions.
ms: Population estimate = 40 × 50 / 10 = 200.
Marks remain identifiable without altering survival or capture probability.
Marked individuals mix randomly.
The population is sufficiently closed over the interval.

parts.q: Calculate reference-population heterozygote frequency under Hardy–Weinberg.
Explain fragmentation effects on diversity and evaluate one management response.
ms: Small groups undergo stronger chance changes through drift.
Isolation reduces gene flow.
Inbreeding increases homozygosity and can expose harmful recessive alleles.
Corridors or carefully managed movement can support gene flow.
Monitor habitat, disease and genetic outcomes rather than assuming movement is always beneficial.
